question: Do image-classification CNNs learn a characteristic layerwise curvature profile, and can the final-layer curvature jump diagnose generalization better than intrinsic dimension?

key_findings.claim: Author-reported profile: selected VGG and ResNet classifiers show an early MAPC jump, an intermediate plateau, and a large final-layer increase, while untrained networks flatten late.
key_findings.evidence: The authors estimate mean absolute principal curvature (MAPC) after selected blocks of VGG13/16/19 and ResNet18/50/101 on CIFAR-10/100. A ten-seed ResNet18 curve spans roughly 1.6e-4 at the input to 3 at the linear output, and the six-model relative-depth plot has a shared qualitative step shape. Randomly initialized VGGs and ResNets instead drop toward zero in later layers. Only the ResNet18 curve visibly carries a ten-seed deviation analysis; the cross-architecture profiles are descriptive rather than an uncertainty-calibrated population claim.

anchors.section: Figure 3, MAPC profiles and neighborhood convergence

key_findings.claim: The estimator measures the network image of an artificial SVD-denoising orbit, not a demonstrated neighborhood on the natural-image data manifold.
key_findings.evidence: For each image, all subsets of its ten smallest singular values are zeroed, producing 2^10=1,024 variants that are then propagated through the network. These one-sided, discrete low-rank edits are chosen because they are Euclidean-close, but no likelihood, semantic-invariance, tangent-consistency, or nearest-real-image test shows that they lie on the natural-image manifold. The cited SVD/PCA theory justifies estimating tangent planes from genuine local samples; it does not establish that deleting singular values creates such samples. Consequently, late MAPC can reflect the network's response to this particular denoising intervention.

key_findings.claim: The local-coordinate construction has a dimension mismatch that the reported rank check does not resolve.
key_findings.evidence: The augmentation is indexed by only ten binary deletion choices, so any smooth interpolation of that generator has intrinsic dimension at most ten. Yet the tangent dimension d is imported from TwoNN on the original, unaugmented layer representation and reaches tens to around one hundred in the appendix plots. A nonlinear image of a finite Boolean cube can have PCA rank above ten, satisfying the paper's r>d check, but that extra affine rank is not evidence for a d-dimensional local tangent. Fitting d-dimensional Hessians to this finite augmentation orbit therefore mixes global nonlinear chords with local tangent directions.

anchors.section: Curvature estimation, TwoNN d and rank-r condition
Figure 9, layerwise IDs up to roughly 110
Figure 11 and Appendix E, d-dimensional PCA frame

key_findings.claim: MAPC is not a canonical higher-codimension curvature scalar and can depend on the estimated normal-frame basis.
key_findings.evidence: For codimension D-d, the method builds one Hessian/shape matrix H-alpha per PCA normal direction, takes each matrix's eigenvalues, and averages their absolute values. Under a rotation of the normal frame, these matrices mix linearly; the sum of their nuclear norms is not generally invariant. Moreover, the spectra of the separate shape operators do not by themselves determine the Riemann tensor because the Gauss equation also depends on component/eigenvector alignment. Appendix G correctly uses the full h-alpha-ij components, so the main-text statement that the Riemann tensor is fully determined by the pooled 'principal curvatures' is too strong.

anchors.section: Curvature estimation, per-normal Hessian eigenvalues and MAPC
Appendix A, acknowledged lack of a canonical scalar curvature metric
Appendix G.3, Gauss equation in full Hessian components

key_findings.claim: The stated second-order approximation has an error term of the same order as the Hessian signal, and the CNN maps are not globally twice differentiable.
key_findings.evidence: Both Section 3 and Appendix E print a second-order Taylor model with remainder O(||u_ij||_2^2); a valid second-order identification normally needs a smaller third-order remainder under sufficient smoothness. As written, the unmodeled error is the same quadratic order as the fitted Hessian. Separately, VGG/ResNet use ReLU and pooling operations, so their feature maps are only piecewise smooth; neighborhoods crossing activation or pooling boundaries contain kinks where a classical Hessian/second fundamental form is undefined. The regression can still return a useful scale-dependent statistic, but it is not automatically Riemannian curvature.

key_findings.claim: Low-dimensional sphere/ellipsoid validation does not stress the high-dimensional, high-codimension, nonsmooth setting used for CNN representations.
key_findings.evidence: CAML implementation is checked on smooth two-dimensional surfaces in R3, where codimension is one, topology is known, samples are genuinely drawn from the surface, and Gaussian curvature is analytic. Figure 2 shows substantial small-sample error before convergence. The real experiments instead use an estimated d, very large D-d, artificial neighborhoods, ReLU networks, and pooled normal directions. No synthetic benchmark varies d, codimension, noise, normal-frame rotation, neighborhood anisotropy, or activation-boundary crossings to establish MAPC calibration in that regime.

key_findings.claim: The normalized last-layer MAPC gap correlates with selected accuracies, but the study does not validate it as a predictor of generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4A contains only three architectures per family and fits separate lines through each trio. Figure 4B uses nested CIFAR-100 subsets c1 through c10i, changing class count, data amount, difficulty, and accuracy together; the points are not independent tasks. There are no correlation coefficients, uncertainty intervals, preregistered threshold, held-out architectures, out-of-sample calibration, or comparison to training accuracy/generalization gap. The outcome is test accuracy, not train-test generalization error, so 'indicator' and 'predicts' are stronger than the evidence.

anchors.section: Section 4.2, NMAPC-gap definition and cumulative-class design

key_findings.claim: MAPC and its gap are representation-coordinate dependent, so functionally equivalent rescalings can alter the proposed diagnostic.
key_findings.evidence: Extrinsic curvature has inverse-length units and changes under non-isometric affine transformations of activation space. A layer can be rescaled and compensated by inverse scaling in the next linear map without changing predictions, yet Euclidean distances, Hessian eigenvalues, and MAPC change. Dividing the last-two-layer difference by the mean MAPC across selected layers is not proven invariant to per-layer scaling, BatchNorm statistics, channel reparameterizations, changing ambient width, or the architecture-specific choice of sampled blocks. Absolute overlap across architectures therefore cannot by itself identify a functional law.

anchors.section: Section 4.1, absolute MAPC comparison across architectures

key_findings.claim: The training-trajectory plot is temporally confounded and does not show that curvature drives accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: One ResNet18 is checkpointed over epochs; both test accuracy and NMAPC gap rise early and then saturate. Epoch, loss reduction, feature scale, and representation separation can jointly drive both quantities. There is no intervention that changes curvature while holding optimization progress fixed, no lagged prediction test, and no comparison of equal-accuracy checkpoints with different gaps. The conclusion that the network 'favors a large gap to increase its performance' is causal language unsupported by this trajectory.

anchors.section: Section 4.4 and Figure 5, single training trajectory

key_findings.claim: The regularizer comparison suggests mixup flattens intermediate representations, but it is not a controlled or replicated test of curvature's role.
key_findings.evidence: The baseline uses weight decay and cosine scheduling, whereas mixup, manifold mixup, and the no-regularizer model are described as having no other regularization. Figure 6C reports accuracies 95.7, 85.5, 95.1, and 90.6 respectively; the manifold-mixup implementation is far below the others. Curves lack seed intervals and simultaneously change augmentation, optimization, performance, activation distribution, and feature scale. The four NMAPC gaps (14,14,13,8) cannot establish that a high final gap is 'fundamental' to success.

anchors.section: Section 4.6 and Figure 6C, regularizer configurations and accuracies

key_findings.claim: The claim that curvature is independent of intrinsic dimension is conditional on unstable estimators that also set the estimator's tangent dimension.
key_findings.evidence: TwoNN, MLE, and persistent-homology estimates differ substantially, while each yields a similar MAPC profile after being substituted as d. This is useful robustness evidence for the plotted shape, but it does not establish statistical independence between true dimension and true curvature. A later AISTATS 2026 analysis proves that common layerwise ID estimators need not track the true ID and can instead follow expansion/neighbor-scale effects. Here, estimator bias propagates into tangent/normal splitting and Hessian count, so agreement of outputs may reflect the pipeline's dominant augmentation/scale signal.

anchors.section: Figure 11, divergent ID and similar MAPC curves

key_findings.claim: The broader ImageNet evidence is a partial extension, not full replication of the main profile or diagnostic.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix trains one ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet and evaluates one ResNet50 on 20,000 images from 100 ImageNet classes. The ImageNet profile has a mild rather than abrupt final jump; no multi-architecture accuracy prediction or seed analysis is shown. Figure 10 changes Tiny-ImageNet class count and depicts a mostly monotone gap decline with accuracy only as color. These results show the computation can be run beyond CIFAR but do not justify 'all datasets, architectures, models, and training protocols.'

anchors.section: Appendix B, Tiny ImageNet and 100-class ImageNet setup

key_findings.claim: The final 'highly curved class peaks facilitate separation' account is a hypothesis, not a mechanism established by the experiments.
key_findings.evidence: The paper observes late-layer curvature statistics and correlates one normalized gap with accuracy, then proposes that samples concentrate near same-class points in highly curved peaks and suggests constructing step-profile models. It does not measure class-conditional curvature, margin, cluster separation, decision-boundary distance, or causal effects of enforcing the profile. A trained final linear projection can itself anisotropically reshape extrinsic curvature without demonstrating cluster concentration.

anchors.section: Section 5, proposed curved-peak interpretation and design suggestion

method.core_idea: Densify each image's purported local manifold with SVD-based variants, propagate that neighborhood through selected CNN layers, fit local quadratic graph embeddings, and summarize their estimated second fundamental forms as a layerwise curvature profile.
method.mechanism: For each image, zero every subset of its ten smallest channel singular values to create 1,024 nearby inputs; estimate a layer's global intrinsic dimension d; use PCA to split each propagated neighborhood into d tangent and D-d normal coordinates; least-squares fit one Hessian per normal coordinate; pool the absolute Hessian eigenvalues into MAPC; compare profiles, a normalized last-layer gap, dimension estimators, checkpoints, initialization states, and regularizers.
assumptions: Natural-image and latent activation distributions are well approximated locally by smooth Riemannian submanifolds.
Deleting small image singular values stays on, or sufficiently close to, the true local data manifold.
The finite 1,024-point augmentation cloud supports the d-dimensional tangent estimate imported from the original dataset.
ReLU/pooling feature maps are sufficiently smooth over each fitted neighborhood for a quadratic curvature approximation.
PCA reliably identifies tangent and normal spaces in high dimension and high codimension.
MAPC is comparable across normal bases, activation scales, layer widths, and architectures.
A correlation with test accuracy across selected models/subsets diagnoses generalization rather than task difficulty or scale.
The final linear layer's curvature change reflects learned representation organization rather than affine reparameterization or estimator behavior.

techniques.role: Create 1,024 per-image variants by deleting combinations of ten small singular values.
Propagate each synthetic neighborhood and collect activations after selected CNN blocks.
Estimate a global intrinsic dimension for the original representation at each layer.
Use local PCA coordinates and least squares to estimate normal-component Hessians.
Pool absolute eigenvalues of all estimated normal-direction Hessians into one scalar.
Normalize the last-two-layer MAPC difference by mean layerwise MAPC as an accuracy correlate.
Place selected layers from networks of different depths on a common 0-to-1 axis.

evaluations.setting: Smooth spheres and ellipsoids in R3 with known Gaussian curvature
evaluations.metric: Estimated Gaussian curvature or relative error versus neighborhood sample count
evaluations.result: The implemented CAML estimator approaches the analytic values as the sample count grows, with visible high variance/error at small counts.
evaluations.baseline: Closed-form codimension-one curvature on clean two-dimensional manifolds.

evaluations.setting: VGG13/16/19 and ResNet18/50/101 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
evaluations.metric: Layerwise MAPC at selected relative depths
evaluations.result: Profiles generally jump early, plateau around 1e-2 to 1e-1, and increase at the final linear layer; a ResNet18 ten-seed curve shows the same shape.
evaluations.baseline: Randomly initialized VGG/ResNet models, whose late-layer estimates collapse toward zero.

evaluations.setting: Six architectures on CIFAR-10/100 and nested ten-step CIFAR-100 class subsets
evaluations.result: Selected points show positive within-family associations, with no reported out-of-sample prediction or formal correlation uncertainty.
evaluations.baseline: Qualitative comparison to prior intrinsic-dimension accuracy indicators.

evaluations.setting: One ResNet18 checkpointed across CIFAR-10 training
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy across epochs colored by NMAPC gap
evaluations.result: Accuracy and the curvature gap rise together early and saturate together.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier checkpoints from the same temporally ordered run.

evaluations.setting: ResNet50 with baseline training, mixup, manifold mixup, or no regularization
evaluations.metric: Layerwise MAPC, normalized final gap, and test accuracy
evaluations.result: Mixup lowers intermediate MAPC by about an order of magnitude while retaining a late jump; no-regularizer has the smallest reported gap and lower accuracy, while manifold mixup has baseline-like curvature but much worse accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: A weight-decayed, cosine-scheduled ResNet50 baseline; configurations are not otherwise matched.

evaluations.setting: ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet and ResNet50 on 20,000 images from 100 ImageNet classes
evaluations.metric: Layerwise ID/MAPC and class-count NMAPC gap
evaluations.result: Tiny ImageNet has a CIFAR-like late rise; the selected ImageNet profile rises overall with only a mild final jump.
evaluations.baseline: CIFAR profiles rather than independent curvature estimators or held-out predictive diagnostics.

evaluations.setting: ResNet50/CIFAR-10 with TwoNN, MLE, and persistent-homology dimension inputs
evaluations.metric: Estimated ID and resulting MAPC profiles
evaluations.result: ID values differ substantially but the broad MAPC step profile remains similar.
evaluations.baseline: Three alternative dimension estimators inside the same augmentation/quadratic-fit pipeline.

limitations: Artificial singular-value deletion is not validated as sampling the natural-image manifold.
Ten binary augmentation factors are inconsistent with the much larger d-dimensional tangent spaces fitted in many layers.
MAPC is not generally invariant to rotations of a high-codimension normal frame or to function-preserving activation rescalings.
The printed second-order approximation uses an O(||u||^2) remainder, which does not separate the fitted quadratic term from approximation error.
ReLU, max-pooling, and related CNN operations produce piecewise-smooth rather than globally C2 representations.
Estimator validation is confined to clean, smooth, two-dimensional codimension-one surfaces.
Cross-model accuracy associations use very few architecture points, nested datasets, and no held-out calibration or formal uncertainty.
Test accuracy is treated as generalization capability without analyzing train-test gaps or equal-training-performance models.
Training dynamics and regularizer comparisons are correlational and confounded by epoch, scale, optimization, and accuracy.
Only one main profile reports ten-seed variation; most cross-architecture/regularizer conclusions lack replication intervals.
ImageNet coverage is one model on 100 classes/20,000 images and does not reproduce the full predictor analysis.
The class-peak mechanism and recommendation to design step-like profiles are speculative rather than intervention-tested.
failure_modes: SVD variants can leave the natural-image manifold while remaining close in pixel Euclidean distance.
Binary one-sided perturbations can turn finite chords or denoising responses into apparent local curvature.
PCA rank after a nonlinear map can exceed the augmentation's true parameter dimension and be mistaken for tangent dimension.
Near-degenerate PCA normal directions can rotate across seeds/layers and change the pooled MAPC.
Neighborhoods crossing ReLU or pooling boundaries can report a scale-dependent kink as Hessian curvature.
Feature rescaling or BatchNorm behavior can alter curvature values without altering model predictions.
Dimension-estimator bias can alter tangent/normal splitting while leaving a superficially robust profile.
A lower-dimensional final classifier projection can create an apparent last-layer jump unrelated to class-manifold concentration.
Nested class-count sweeps can generate accuracy correlations through task difficulty alone.
A regularizer can change activation magnitude and augmentation sensitivity rather than the semantic geometry of representations.
reusable_insights: Separate extrinsic curvature, intrinsic curvature, decision-boundary curvature, and parameter-loss curvature explicitly.
Validate data-manifold neighborhoods with likelihood, semantic preservation, real-neighbor overlap, and augmentation-family sensitivity.
Match synthetic estimator tests to the real task's intrinsic dimension, codimension, noise, nonsmoothness, and sampling anisotropy.
Prefer coordinate-invariant curvature functionals or report sensitivity to normal-frame rotations and activation reparameterizations.
Test a geometry diagnostic prospectively on held-out architectures/datasets and against train-test gap, margins, calibration, and simple scale baselines.
Use interventions that alter curvature while matching accuracy, feature norm, optimizer progress, and representation dimension before making causal claims.
Report neighborhood-radius convergence, regression residuals, condition numbers, and per-sample uncertainty for local quadratic estimators.
Treat the augmentation parameter dimension as an upper bound on any tangent dimension inferred from its local orbit.
open_questions: Does the step profile persist with genuine nearest-neighbor, learned generative, diffusion-augmented, and domain-valid continuous neighborhoods?
Is there a normal-frame- and scale-invariant curvature statistic that predicts held-out generalization across architectures?
How much of the final jump is caused by the linear classifier projection, output dimension, activation scale, or class separation?
What curvature is well-defined for piecewise-linear representation maps at activation-region boundaries?
Can one estimate class-conditional rather than pooled data-manifold curvature and relate it causally to margins?
Do transformer, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and non-vision representations show the same profile under matched estimators?
How do true local dimension, estimator bias, normal codimension, and neighborhood radius jointly affect MAPC?
Can explicit curvature regularization improve classification after matching feature norms and all other training choices?
Does the NMAPC gap predict generalization error prospectively beyond parameter count, training loss, feature norm, and class count?

competitive_landscape.title: Curvature-based Comparison of Two Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Yu et al. already generate per-sample neighborhoods and estimate Riemann/sectional curvature to compare activation manifolds. Kaufman and Azencot adapt that core procedure to convolutional layer profiles, many architectures, regularizers, and an accuracy-gap proposal; novelty is the systematic application and empirical profile, not local curvature estimation itself.

competitive_landscape.title: The Riemannian Geometry of Deep Generative Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Shao et al. use an explicit differentiable generator parameterization and report image-generator manifolds surprisingly near zero curvature. The reviewed work studies discriminative activation point clouds and finds high late curvature, but its implicit-manifold/SVD estimator makes the apparent disagreement inseparable from architecture, object, and measurement choice.

competitive_landscape.title: Intrinsic dimension of data representations in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Ansuini et al. establish the hunchback ID profile and late-layer ID/accuracy association and explicitly conjecture low-dimensional but nonflat manifolds. Kaufman and Azencot directly target that nonflatness with curvature estimates, but inherit ID-estimator and cross-architecture correlation concerns.

competitive_landscape.title: Intrinsic Dimension, Persistent Homology and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Birdal et al. derive topology-based generalization bounds and an efficient persistent-homology dimension estimator. The reviewed NMAPC gap is an empirical activation-space correlate without a bound or prospective prediction, though its curvature focus can capture information dimension alone omits.

competitive_landscape.title: On the geometry of generalization and memorization in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Stephenson et al. analyze object-manifold radius/dimension, localize memorization to later layers, and validate a causal prediction by reverting late-layer weights. Kaufman and Azencot add an extrinsic-curvature profile but do not intervene on curvature or disentangle it from layer progression.

competitive_landscape.title: How does training shape the Riemannian geometry of neural network representations?
competitive_landscape.difference: Zavatone-Veth et al. study the pullback metric induced by feature maps, derive an infinite-width random baseline, and show feature learning magnifies regions near decision boundaries across supervised and self-supervised models. This supplies theory and boundary-local analysis absent from MAPC, while MAPC instead summarizes layerwise extrinsic bending of an estimated data manifold.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantifying Extrinsic Curvature in Neural Manifolds
competitive_landscape.difference: Acosta et al. learn an explicit topological parameterization, prove selected invariances, and validate on noisy deformed circles, spheres, tori, and real neural data. Their validation better matches high-dimensional point-cloud curvature than the reviewed codimension-one check, though the domain is biological activity rather than CNN image representations.

competitive_landscape.title: On Explicit Curvature Regularization in Deep Generative Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Lee and Park derive coordinate-invariant intrinsic/extrinsic curvature functionals from an explicit decoder and intervene on them during training, finding a nonmonotone regularization tradeoff. This is a stronger causal design than correlating MAPC with accuracy and cautions that neither simply larger nor smaller curvature is universally desirable.

competitive_landscape.title: Curvature Estimation on Data Manifolds via Diffusion-augmented Sampling
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. directly address sparse/noisy curvature estimation by learning a diffusion model and sampling a denser manifold neighborhood, with heterogeneous synthetic-manifold comparisons to raw-data estimators. It targets the reviewed paper's central unvalidated SVD-neighborhood assumption, while adding dependence on generative-model fidelity.

competitive_landscape.title: Rethinking Intrinsic Dimension Estimation in Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Schulte and Rügamer show theoretically and empirically that common neural-representation ID estimators do not track true ID and identify expansion/neighbor-scale effects behind familiar profiles. Because the reviewed method uses such estimates to choose tangent dimension, this later result makes its ID-versus-curvature independence and local-coordinate validity substantially less secure.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximating Latent Manifolds in Neural Networks via Vanishing Ideals
competitive_landscape.difference: Pelleriti et al. approximate class manifolds with polynomial vanishing ideals and turn the approximation into a shallower classifier with spectral generalization analysis. It makes the manifold model operational and class-specific, whereas the reviewed MAPC profile is a pooled post-hoc scalar without a predictive theorem or architecture intervention.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Deep image classifiers share a three-phase curvature profile, unlike untrained networks; a normalized final-layer curvature gap tracks performance, dimension need not reveal curvature, and mixup selectively flattens intermediate representations.
novelty_assessment.evidence: CAML-style quadratic estimates on SVD-augmented neighborhoods yield similar profiles for six CNN architectures on CIFAR, selected Tiny-ImageNet/ImageNet extensions, trained/untrained comparisons, one checkpoint trajectory, three ID estimators, and four training/regularization configurations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Systematically plotting a curvature-like statistic across common CNN layers and contrasting it with intrinsic dimension was a useful empirical extension of prior activation-manifold work. The strongest contribution is the reproducible descriptive profile and a set of testable hypotheses. The paper does not yet establish actual natural-image-manifold curvature or a generalization predictor: its ten-factor artificial neighborhood conflicts with fitted dimensions, MAPC is noncanonical and reparameterization-sensitive in high codimension, smoothness/Taylor assumptions fail as written, correlations are small/confounded, and contemporary/later work offers explicit invariant parameterizations, causal curvature regularization, diffusion-based density, and a foundational critique of ID estimators.

reviewer_notes: All 18 pages of the recovered official ICML 2023 PMLR version were read. Figure-heavy pages 4-9 and 13-17 were visually inspected, confirming the printed O(||u||^2) Taylor remainder, small/cumulative accuracy panels, regularizer accuracies, ImageNet scope, and ID-estimator curves. Primary competitors were checked on official arXiv, OpenReview, NeurIPS, and PMLR records on 2026-08-23. The atlas's malformed legacy title was resolved to the exact published title 'Data Representations’ Study of Latent Image Manifolds'; the stable OpenReview identifier was preserved.
